summary: Segment Routing P2MP Policies define explicit multicast paths, installed via a controller, NETCONF/YANG, or a command line. This Standards Track document defines how to use ping-style (MPLS OAM) checks to verify these policies in MPLS Segment Routing networks.

eli5.summary: After building a delivery tree, you shout down the branches to check every branch reaches its end.

questions: how to test sr p2mp policy
what is sr p2mp policy ping
how to traceroute an sr p2mp tree
what is sub-tlv 41 in mpls ping
subtitle: How to ping and traceroute a Segment Routing multicast tree to find where it breaks.

tldr.problem: A Segment Routing P2MP Policy is installed by a controller, NETCONF/YANG or a CLI, with no underlay signaling protocol to distribute it, so finding where a multicast tree fails to deliver traffic is hard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the MPLS P2MP ping and traceroute procedures of RFC 6425 and adds one new Target FEC Stack sub-TLV (sub-type 41) that names the Root, Tree-ID and Instance-ID of the tree instance under test.
tldr.outcome: Operators can check each candidate path and tree instance from the Root, and run a traceroute to localize a fault after a ping fails. It applies to MPLS only, not SRv6.

today: RFC 9961 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2026. The unit metadata shows it neither obsoletes nor updates another RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What Is Being Tested
sections.content:
An SR P2MP Policy (see RFC 9960) has candidate paths (CPs), and a CP may hold several P2MP tree instances (PTIs). A PTI is the actual P2MP tunnel from the Root to a set of Leaves through transit routers. Several PTIs let a network switch from an active tree to a newly optimized one with Make-Before-Break.

This RFC specifies a way to detect data plane failures in a CP and its PTIs, for both active and backup paths. It applies only to Replication Segments that use MPLS encapsulation and does not cover SRv6. It builds on RFC 6425, and all considerations and limitations in Section 6 of that RFC apply here too.
sections.eli5: A delivery tree can have several versions of itself. This RFC says how to check any one of them to see if it works.

sections.title: Why Ping and Traceroute Are Needed
sections.content:
The policy and its Replication segments are normally provisioned by a central controller or by NETCONF/YANG or CLI. The Root and Leaves are discovered as in RFC 9960 and the tree is computed from the Root to the Leaves. There is no underlay signaling protocol that distributes the policy from the Root to the Leaves, so a tree that fails to deliver user traffic is hard to diagnose without these tools.

The intended workflow is simple. Periodic pings verify connectivity between the Root and the Leaves. If a ping fails, a traceroute finds the point of failure along the tree. Both can be started from the node responsible for establishing the policy.
sections.eli5: Nobody tells the branches of the tree where they fit, so when a branch goes quiet you need a way to poke it and see where the message stops.

sections.title: Reusing the RFC 6425 Procedures
sections.content:
Ping and traceroute packets follow the SR P2MP Policy on a chosen CP and PTI toward the Leaves, and are replicated at each replication point using the Replication segment forwarding information. They are handled as ordinary MPLS packets when the TTL expires or they reach a Leaf, and the response goes back to the Root as RFC 6425 describes. The same destination UDP port as in RFC 8029 is reused.

Three things differ from other P2MP MPLS protocols:

  • Egress Address P2MP Responder sub-TLVs SHOULD NOT be used in an echo request carrying an SR P2MP Policy FEC, because transit routers do not know the Leaf nodes. A node that receives them will not respond.
  • End of traceroute: the Root knows the Leaves, so it can tell when processing is done and a configurable upper limit on TTL may not be necessary. Having one is an implementation choice.
  • Identifying the path under test: a new Target FEC Stack sub-TLV is introduced for CPs and PTIs.

Implementations MUST account for multiple CPs per policy and multiple PTIs per CP, and SHOULD support testing each one individually. A downstream node that understands the Replication-SID MUST process the request and respond even when that CP and PTI are not the active path.
sections.eli5: The old way of checking multicast roads mostly works here too. The Root already knows everyone on the tree, so it knows when the check is finished, and every version of the tree must answer even if it is not the one in use.

sections.title: Interworking with Unicast Paths
sections.content:
RFC 9960 allows two ways to build a tree: with adjacent Replication segments or with non-adjacent ones. For adjacent segments there is nothing special about TTL handling, and the TTL is decremented hop by hop.

For non-adjacent segments, for example two joined by an SR Policy, the P2MP OAM tools verify the Replication segments, while unicast OAM tools verify the unicast path between them. The Replication-SID should not be exposed or examined in that unicast path. TTL handling depends on the MPLS TTL mode (Pipe or Uniform, per RFC 3270). For traceroute the TTL mode MUST be Pipe Mode on the router where the unicast path starts, so the packet can reach the downstream Replication segment. For ping, either mode may be used. Detecting failures of the unicast path itself is out of scope.
sections.eli5: When two parts of the tree are joined by an ordinary road, you test the tree parts with this tool and the ordinary road with the ordinary tools, and you tell the traceroute not to run out of time on that road.

sections.title: The Tree Instance Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The packet format follows Section 3 of RFC 8029. To identify the segment being tested, the echo request MUST include a Target FEC Stack TLV that names the CP and PTI. This RFC adds the SR MPLS P2MP Policy Tree Instance sub-TLV, sub-type 41, with a variable length. Its value follows Section 2.3 of RFC 9960. The sub-TLV tests one specific PTI within a CP, not the CP as a whole.

The value holds an Address Family (2 octets, IPv4 or IPv6 only), an Address Length (1 octet, 4 for IPv4 and 16 for IPv6), a Reserved octet that MUST be zero when sent and is ignored on receipt, the Root address, a 4-octet Tree-ID and a 2-octet Instance-ID.
sections.eli5: To ask about one particular version of the tree, the message carries a name tag: who the root is, which tree it is, and which version of it.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned sub-type 41, named SR MPLS P2MP Policy Tree Instance, in the "Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21" registry under the MPLS LSPs Ping Parameters registry group. It was taken from the Standards Action range of 0-16383, and it sits under Type 1 (Target FEC Stack).
sections.eli5: The official list of tag numbers now has an entry, number 41, for this new tag.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The security needs are the same as in RFC 9960, RFC 6425 and RFC 8029. SR P2MP Policy ping is open to the same three attack vectors described in Section 5 of RFC 8029, and the same mitigations should be applied. The RFC also points to the advice from RFC 4379 via RFC 6425: to avoid denial-of-service attacks, implementations are RECOMMENDED to regulate LSP ping traffic going to the control plane, and a rate limiter SHOULD be applied to the well-known UDP port.
sections.eli5: Anyone could flood a router with check messages, so routers should only answer a limited number per second.
